lessons.title: Choosing a deployment unit
lessons.summary: Compare monoliths, modular monoliths and microservices without confusing deployment units with instance counts.
lessons.body:
Every system has to answer one structural question early: **how many separately deployable pieces should it have?** The answer shapes how teams work, how failures spread, how fast you can ship and how much your infrastructure costs.

There are three broad shapes. None of them is "best". Each is a different set of trade-offs.

## The three shapes

```
 Monolith        Modular monolith
+----------+     +----------------+
| UI       |     | [Orders ]      |
| Orders   |     | [Billing]      |
| Billing  |     | [Catalog]      |
| Catalog  |     |  one process   |
+----+-----+     +-------+--------+
     |                   |
   [ DB ]              [ DB ]
                    (schema per module)

 Microservices
[Orders]   [Billing]   [Catalog]
   |           |           |
 [DB1]       [DB2]       [DB3]
```

- **Monolith**: an application deployed as one unit (often replicated behind a load balancer). Modules commonly call each other in-process and may share a database; a particular repository layout or exactly one database is not required.
- **Modular monolith**: still one deployable, but the code is split into modules with **enforced boundaries**: each module owns its tables, exposes a public interface, and other modules may not reach into its internals. Shopify has described a gradual effort to create boundaries within its large Rails monolith; such migrations do not establish complete isolation overnight.
- **Microservices**: each business capability is its own service with its own process, its own deployment pipeline and, crucially, **its own data**. Services talk over the network (HTTP/gRPC or messages).

## What a monolith gives you for free

It's easy to undersell the monolith. Inside one process you get:

- **Function calls instead of network calls.** An ordinary call avoids network transport latency and uncertainty about remote delivery. The function can still block, throw after partial state changes, or be interrupted by a process crash; local calls are not automatically atomic.
- **ACID transactions across features.** Placing an order and decrementing stock can be one database transaction.
- **Simple refactoring.** Renaming an interface is an IDE operation, not a multi-team API migration.
- **One thing to deploy, monitor and debug.** A stack trace can show an in-process call chain; asynchronous work and external dependencies still need tracing or correlated logs.

The costs show up with scale, of the *organisation* more than of traffic:

- Build and test times grow; a 40-minute CI pipeline slows everyone.
- A bad release can affect the whole application; staged deployment and isolation can limit the impact.
- Everything scales together. If image resizing needs 30 CPU-heavy boxes, you run 30 copies of the whole app.
- Without discipline, the code becomes a "big ball of mud" where everything depends on everything.

> [!note] A monolith still scales horizontally
> "Monolith" describes the deployment unit, not the instance count. Running 50 stateless copies of one app behind a load balancer is normal and handles very high traffic.

## Key takeaways
- A monolith is one deployable, which can run as many stateless instances.
- A modular monolith enforces internal interfaces and data ownership while retaining one deployable.
- In-process calls and shared local transactions simplify coordination, but organisation size and uneven workloads can expose costs.

## Further reading
- [Martin Fowler: Microservices](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html)
- [microservices.io: Monolithic architecture pattern](https://microservices.io/patterns/monolithic.html)

questions.prompt: Which statement about a monolithic architecture is accurate?

options.text: A monolith can only ever run as a single server instance.
options.explanation: Wrong. 'Monolith' describes the deployment unit (one build, one process type), not the instance count. Stateless monoliths routinely run as dozens of identical copies behind a load balancer.

options.text: Modules in a monolith communicate over HTTP, just like microservices.
options.explanation: Modules can use in-process calls without remote transport failure modes. Local calls can still throw, partially mutate state or be interrupted by a crash.

options.text: A monolith is deployed as one unit, and its modules can share a single ACID transaction.
options.explanation: Correct. One deployable with one database means placing an order and decrementing stock can be a single transaction, which is much harder once those live in separate services with separate databases.

options.text: A monolith cannot be split into internal modules with enforced boundaries.
options.explanation: Wrong. A modular monolith can enforce internal interfaces and data ownership within one deployable. Shopify describes a gradual migration toward this structure; its tooling does not prove every boundary is enforced.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate two ideas: *how many deployables* and *how many instances*.
2. A monolith has one deployable. You can still run 50 copies of it.
3. Within the process, calls are function calls, and all modules can share one database.
4. Sharing one database means a single transaction can span features: `BEGIN; INSERT order; UPDATE stock; COMMIT;`.
5. So the accurate statement is the one about a single deployable plus cross-module ACID transactions.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a **modular monolith** from an ordinary monolith?

options.text: It runs each module in a separate container.
options.explanation: Separate containers do not define a modular monolith, and they do not automatically establish microservice independence. The defining distinction is enforced module boundaries within one deployment unit.

options.text: Its modules have enforced boundaries: each owns its own tables and exposes a public interface, and other modules can't reach into its internals.
options.explanation: Correct. It keeps one build and one deploy, but adds the discipline of service-like boundaries, often checked by tooling.

options.text: It uses a separate database server per module.
options.explanation: Wrong. It may use a schema per module, but the defining feature is enforced code and data boundaries, not separate servers.

options.text: It can only be scaled vertically.
options.explanation: Wrong. Like any monolith, it can run many identical copies behind a load balancer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Deployment shape alone does not tell you how strongly internal boundaries are enforced.
2. A modular monolith makes module interfaces and data ownership explicit within one deployment unit.
3. Checks can reject forbidden dependencies. Shopify's Packwerk checks static constant references, but ignores method calls and can miss violations; a tool alone does not enforce every data boundary.
4. Explicit dependencies can make later extraction easier, although operational and data-migration work remains.

lessons.title: The cost of service independence
lessons.summary: Model required-service availability and see why separate data owners change transaction design.
lessons.body:
The previous unit distinguished deployment shapes. This unit asks what changes when a call crosses the network and each service owns its database.

## What microservices buy, and what they cost

Microservices let **teams** move independently:

- Each team deploys on its own schedule, without coordinating a release train.
- Services scale independently: the search service gets 40 instances, the admin service gets 2.
- Technology can differ where it matters (a Go service for a latency-critical path, Python for ML).
- A failure can be contained: if recommendations are down, checkout can still work, *if* you designed for it.

The cost is that you've turned a single program into a **distributed system**:

| Concern | Monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|
| Call cost | No network transport; can fail | Adds transport and partial failures |
| Transactions | Local ACID can span modules | Local ACID; coordination across owners |
| Debugging | Stack trace | Distributed tracing |
| Deploys | 1 pipeline | N pipelines |
| Data joins | SQL JOIN | API calls or copies |

Every network hop adds latency and a new failure mode. When a request needs *every* service in a chain to work, the chances multiply: the request succeeds only if service 1 works **and** service 2 works **and** so on. Assuming the services fail independently of each other, the combined availability is:

```formula reference
A_total = A_1 × A_2 × ... × A_n
A_total = A^n
where
A_total: the fraction of requests (or time) for which the whole chain works, between 0 and 1 (0.994 = 99.4 %)
A_1: the availability of the first required service, a fraction between 0 and 1
A_2: the availability of the second required service, likewise
...: and so on, one factor per required service
A_n: the availability of the last (nth) required service
A: the availability of each service when they are all the same, e.g. 0.999 (99.9 %); the second line is the shortcut for that case
n: the number of services the request must pass through, all of which must succeed
^: "to the power of": A^n means n copies of A multiplied together
%: per cent; 99.9 % = 0.999
In words: the chain is only as available as all its links together, so an extra fallible required service can lower overall availability.
```

This is a simplified model: it assumes failures are independent (in reality, a shared database or network outage can take several services down together) and that every service is strictly required. Carefully designed fallbacks can reduce required dependencies; retries can also amplify overload, and timeouts only bound waiting rather than guarantee success. You now need service discovery, distributed tracing, centralised logging, contract testing and a platform team to run it all.

### Coordinating a business transaction

An order and a stock reservation can share one local ACID transaction before extraction. With separate Orders and Inventory databases, and no distributed atomic-commit protocol, a **saga** coordinates several local transactions instead.

Orders first creates a pending order and an outbox record in one local transaction. A relay publishes the event; Inventory reserves stock and publishes its outcome reliably. Orders confirms the order, or cancels it through a compensating action if reservation fails. The business must accept the intermediate pending state. Handlers need idempotency, retries and reconciliation, including failed compensation; compensation is an explicit business action rather than automatic isolation or rollback.

A **transactional outbox** makes the business change and the pending event durable together. The relay can publish a duplicate after a crash, so consumers still need deduplication.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A journey with connections
> A journey requiring several connecting trains fails if any required connection is missed.
>
> **How it maps:** Each required service is a necessary connection; adding one adds another condition for the overall request to succeed.
>
> **Where it stops:** Train failures may share a cause, just as services can share infrastructure. The comparison does not justify treating failures as independent.

## Key takeaways
- Independent deployment and scaling require deliberate failure isolation; separation alone does not provide it.
- More required dependencies add failure conditions; a simple availability product requires independent failures.
- A saga coordinates local transactions and compensation; reliable publication and reconciliation remain necessary.

## Further reading
- [Martin Fowler: Microservices](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html)
- [microservices.io: Saga pattern](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html)
- [microservices.io: Transactional outbox](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)

questions.prompt: A checkout succeeds only when every required service responds successfully. You add another required synchronous service with its own failure risk and no fallback. What changes?

options.text: The effect is always exactly the new service’s annual downtime.
options.explanation: Failure overlap, retries and dependency behaviour determine the combined effect; a fixed annual total is not implied.

options.text: The checkout gains another way to fail; independent service availability can estimate the effect, but shared failures need a different model.
options.explanation: Correct. Every required link must work. Correlated outages break a simple product model.

options.text: Availability improves because there are now more services.
options.explanation: More required links are not redundant alternatives; failure of any required link can fail checkout.

options.text: Only the new service’s availability matters.
options.explanation: Checkout still requires the existing services as well.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify which results are required for success.
2. Adding a required result adds a failure condition.
3. An independent-link model can estimate combined availability; shared infrastructure failures violate its assumption.
4. Reduce unnecessary synchronous dependencies or design a valid fallback rather than counting extra services as redundancy.

questions.prompt: In a monolith, placing an order inserts the order and decrements stock in one transaction. After splitting into Orders and Inventory services with separate databases, without a distributed atomic-commit protocol, which pattern can coordinate the business process?

options.text: A distributed lock held across both databases while each writes.
options.explanation: Wrong. A lock doesn't give atomicity: if one write succeeds and the other fails, you still have inconsistent data.

options.text: A saga: Orders creates a pending order and emits an event; Inventory reserves stock; if reservation fails, a compensating action cancels the order. Events are published reliably, for example with an outbox.
options.explanation: Correct. The local transaction commits business state and an outbox row together; a relay publishes later and may publish duplicates. Compensation is another fallible business action, not atomic rollback.

options.text: Nothing; network calls between services are reliable enough not to need it.
options.explanation: Wrong. Partial failure is the defining property of distributed systems; without a plan you'll oversell stock or lose orders.

options.text: Have both services share one database so the transaction still works.
options.explanation: It contradicts the scenario's separate-database premise and introduces shared data coupling. Shared storage does not literally turn separate processes into one service.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before: `BEGIN; INSERT order; UPDATE stock; COMMIT;` All or nothing.
2. After: separate databases with no shared atomic-commit protocol in this scenario.
3. Saga:
   - Orders: insert `PENDING` + outbox event in one local transaction.
   - Inventory: reserve stock, emit `StockReserved` or `StockRejected`.
   - Orders: `CONFIRMED`, or `CANCELLED` (compensation).
4. In between, the order is visibly pending: the business must accept that intermediate state. Make handlers idempotent, publish each transition reliably, and retry or reconcile failed compensation.
5. This is the real price of the split.

lessons.title: Drawing boundaries around capabilities
lessons.summary: Use team communication, feature changes and data ownership to decide whether a service should exist.
lessons.body:
Services offer independent ownership only when their boundaries fit how the business and teams work. Use the costs from the previous unit to evaluate a proposed extraction.

## Conway's law

Melvin Conway's 1968 observation is that an organisation's communication structure constrains the systems it designs. If payments and checkout teams rarely communicate, their service interface may be harder to coordinate and change.

This works in both directions:

- **Descriptive**: communication patterns constrain and influence architecture; this is an organizational observation, not a deterministic prediction from team count.
- **Prescriptive** (the "inverse Conway manoeuvre"): design the team structure you want the architecture to have. If you want an independent search service, create a team that owns search end to end.

The deepest reason to adopt microservices is organisational: they let you give a team **full ownership** of a capability, including its data and on-call. With 8 engineers, that benefit is small. With 400, it can be decisive.

## When to split

Martin Fowler's "Monolith First" advice is widely followed: start with a well-structured monolith, learn where the real boundaries are, then extract services when you have a concrete reason. Good reasons include:

1. **Team contention.** Many teams are blocked on each other's deploys or merge conflicts in one codebase.
2. **Different scaling profiles.** One component (video transcoding, search indexing) needs very different hardware or scale.
3. **Different reliability or security needs.** Card handling might need PCI isolation; a flaky experimental feature shouldn't share a process with checkout.
4. **Different change rates.** A pricing engine that changes daily next to a ledger that changes yearly.

Bad reasons: "Netflix does it", "it's modern", or a CV-driven rewrite.

### Finding the boundaries

Business capabilities (orders, billing, inventory) can guide boundaries. A DDD bounded context is the scope in which a domain model and its language are consistent; it is not simply a synonym for a capability or necessarily one service. Avoid mechanically splitting every technical layer into a service. A "database service" or "validation service" that every request passes through couples everything to it.

A good boundary has **high cohesion inside, low coupling outside**: most changes touch one service, and services exchange a small number of well-defined messages.

Three practical tests for a proposed service:

- **Can it be deployed alone?** If releasing it usually means releasing a neighbour too, the boundary is wrong.
- **Does it own its data?** No other service writes its tables, and nobody else reads them directly.
- **Does a typical feature stay inside it?** Look at the last 20 features and count how many services each would have touched.

Size matters less than these. "Micro" is about independence, not line count. A service per table often fragments a capability and increases coordination. Evaluate the actual change and data-access boundaries rather than using table count as a rule.

When one service needs another's data, it either calls the owner's API at request time (simple, but couples availability and adds latency) or keeps a **local copy** fed by the owner's events (fast and independent, but eventually consistent). Joins that used to be one SQL query become one of those two choices.

### Making a local copy dependable

For frequently read customer names and loyalty tiers that rarely change, Orders can keep a read model fed by customer events when the page accepts delayed visibility. It needs a bootstrap snapshot, deletion handling, monitored lag and a repair path. Duplicate delivery must be idempotent, and versions or defined ordering must prevent older complete snapshots from replacing newer ones. A credit limit instead needs the authoritative owner to atomically validate and reserve credit: a fresh read followed by a separate write can still race.

## Key takeaways
- Conway's law is an organisational observation, not an exact service-count prediction.
- Extract a capability for a concrete deployment, scaling, security or ownership need.
- Strong boundaries keep most feature changes local and expose data through an owner's interface or events.
- A local read copy trades request-time independence for delayed visibility; it is unsuitable for independently enforcing a credit limit.

## Further reading
- [Martin Fowler: Monolith First](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MonolithFirst.html)
- [Martin Fowler: Conway's Law](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ConwaysLaw.html)

questions.prompt: A company has four teams who barely communicate with each other. According to **Conway's law**, what is the most likely outcome when they build a product together?

options.text: Communication boundaries are likely to influence component boundaries; roughly one major area per team is a plausible outcome, not a guaranteed count
options.explanation: Conway’s observation predicts that communication boundaries influence software boundaries; it does not determine an exact number of components.

options.text: The system will be a single, tightly integrated component, because they share one product.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sharing a product goal doesn't override communication structure. Tight integration requires frequent communication, which these teams lack.

options.text: The system's structure will be determined purely by the technology stack chosen.
options.explanation: Wrong. Conway's observation is precisely that organisational structure, not technology choice, drives system structure.

options.text: Conway's law only applies to compilers, so it says nothing here.
options.explanation: Wrong. Conway's paper used compilers as an example, but the law is a general observation about any system designed by an organisation.

questions.workedExample:
1. Conway's law: *system structure mirrors the organisation's communication structure*.
2. Here: four teams, little communication between them.
3. Each team will build what it can own without negotiating with others, so component boundaries may resemble team boundaries; the law does not calculate an exact number.
4. Where teams rarely talk, the interfaces between their components can become harder to negotiate and change.
5. Practical lesson (the inverse Conway manoeuvre): if you want a different architecture, change the team structure to match it.

questions.prompt: A 12-engineer startup runs one Rails monolith. Deploys take 10 minutes and the team ships several times a day. The CTO wants to move to microservices "to be ready for scale". There's no specific pain today. What's the best recommendation?

options.text: Split into microservices now, one per database table, so each is small and simple.
options.explanation: Wrong. Splitting by table creates services with very low cohesion that must call each other constantly, the textbook route to a distributed monolith.

options.text: Rewrite the whole system as microservices in a new codebase, then switch over in one go.
options.explanation: Wrong. Big-bang rewrites are high risk: the old system keeps changing, the new one lags behind, and cut-over day is a single huge failure point.

options.text: Keep the monolith but enforce module boundaries (each module owns its tables and exposes an interface), and extract a service only when a concrete need appears.
options.explanation: Correct. Explicit boundaries can reduce future extraction work; network, data and operational changes can still make extraction expensive.

options.text: Keep the monolith exactly as it is; microservices never make sense.
options.explanation: Wrong. Microservices do make sense under real pressures such as many teams or very different scaling needs. The advice is to prepare boundaries, not to rule splitting out.

questions.workedExample:
1. List the current pains: none. Deploys are fast and frequent with 12 engineers.
2. List what microservices would add: network calls, distributed transactions, N pipelines, tracing, on-call for many services.
3. The main benefit, independent team ownership, barely applies with one or two teams.
4. But scale may come, so lower the future cost of splitting:
   - Group code into modules by business capability.
   - Give each module its own schema and public interface.
   - Add lint or CI checks that block cross-module internals.
5. When a concrete reason appears (say notifications needs burst scaling), extract that module with the strangler fig pattern.

questions.prompt: A company with 300 engineers has 120 microservices. They notice that most features require changes to 4–5 services owned by different teams, and every feature needs cross-team meetings. What's the most likely root cause, and what fixes it?

options.text: Services are too large; split each into smaller services to reduce coordination.
options.explanation: Wrong. Making services smaller would spread each feature across even more services and teams, increasing coordination.

options.text: Boundaries were drawn along technical layers or the wrong domain lines; redraw them along business capabilities and align team ownership to match.
options.explanation: Correct. If most changes cut across many services, cohesion is low. Realigning services and teams to business capabilities (an inverse Conway manoeuvre) means most features touch one team's services.

options.text: The teams use different programming languages; standardising on one language fixes coordination.
options.explanation: Wrong. Language diversity affects hiring and tooling, but it doesn't cause features to span services. The coupling is in the boundaries, not the language.

options.text: They need a faster network so synchronous calls between services are cheaper.
options.explanation: Wrong. The problem is organisational and design coupling (who must change what), not network latency.

questions.workedExample:
1. Symptom: a typical feature changes 4–5 services owned by different teams.
2. A good boundary means *most changes stay inside one service*. Here they don't, so cohesion is low.
3. Common causes: splitting by technical layer (an API service, a validation service, a data service) or by noun/table instead of capability.
4. Conway's law says team structure and service structure reinforce each other, so fixing one without the other drifts back.
5. Fix: map the business capabilities, merge or redraw services around them, and give each team end-to-end ownership.
6. Measure success: the share of features that need more than one team should fall.

questions.prompt: A 150-engineer company runs one monolith. Which of these are good, concrete reasons to extract a particular component into a service? Select all that apply.

options.text: Eight teams queue behind a single release train, and a bug in one team's code regularly blocks everyone's deploy.
options.explanation: Correct. Team contention on deploys is the classic organisational reason to split.

options.text: A PDF rendering component needs 40 CPU-heavy instances at month end, while the rest of the app needs 6.
options.explanation: Correct. Very different scaling profiles mean you're paying to run 40 copies of the whole app for one component's sake.

options.text: The organization has a concrete requirement to isolate card-data handling behind controlled process and network boundaries
options.explanation: Correct. A specific isolation requirement can justify extraction; merely naming a service or using a separate process does not establish compliance or remove connected systems from scope.

options.text: A conference talk said microservices are the modern way to build software.
options.explanation: Wrong. Fashion isn't a concrete pain. You'd take on distributed-systems costs without a matching benefit.

options.text: Each database table should be its own service so that services are small.
options.explanation: Wrong. Table-per-service creates chatty, tightly coupled services. Boundaries belong at business capabilities.

questions.workedExample:
1. For each option, ask: what pain does extraction remove?
2. Release contention → independent deploys. Yes.
3. PDF scaling: 40 whole-app copies vs 6 + 40 small workers. Yes.
4. Required card-data isolation: extraction may help implement the approved security boundary. Yes; compliance scope requires separate assessment.
5. 'Modern': no pain named. No.
6. Table-per-service: increases coupling. No.

questions.prompt: After splitting, Orders needs each customer's name and loyalty tier (owned by the Customers service) to render every order page, at 2,000 requests per second. Customer details change rarely. What's the usual choice, and its trade-off? The page may show an out-of-date loyalty tier and does not use it to authorize payment or enforce a credit limit.

options.text: Let Orders query the Customers database directly with a SQL join.
options.explanation: Wrong. Reading another service's tables couples the two schemas, which is the shared-database trap.

options.text: Call Customers synchronously on every order page.
options.explanation: Wrong as the usual choice here. It works, but adds a hop and ties Orders' availability to Customers' at 2,000 req/s for data that rarely changes.

options.text: Merge Customers back into Orders.
options.explanation: Wrong. Merging fixes genuinely over-split services, but customer data is used by many capabilities, so one consumer's need isn't a reason.

options.text: Keep a local read model updated by customer events, accepting delayed visibility and handling duplicate or out-of-order events
options.explanation: Correct with the stated stale-read tolerance. Orders can read its copy during an owner outage, but lag has no automatic seconds-level bound.

questions.workedExample:
1. Read path: 2,000 req/s, data rarely changes. That favours a local copy.
2. Owner publishes `CustomerUpdated {id, name, tier}`.
3. Orders consumes it and upserts its own `customer_view` table.
4. Orders' page is a local read: no synchronous Customers call, though it still depends on its own read store and eventually on reliable updates.
5. Trade-off: replication lag that must be monitored; outages can make it arbitrarily long. Bootstrap, deletion and repair paths also matter.
6. For a credit limit, ask the authoritative owner to atomically authorize/reserve against its state. A separate synchronous read followed by a write can still race.

lessons.title: Extracting an independent service safely
lessons.summary: Use gradual routing and data migration while checking for the distributed-monolith failure mode.
lessons.body:
The previous unit identified capability boundaries. Now follow one capability into a separate deployable without losing data ownership or a workable rollback.

### How to split safely: the strangler fig

Rewriting from scratch is risky. The **strangler fig** pattern extracts gradually:

```
           +-----------+
 client -->|  routing  |
           +--+-----+--+
   /billing/* |     | everything else
              v     v
       [Billing svc] [Monolith]
```

1. Introduce a routing or interface boundary around the capability.
2. Build the replacement and establish data ownership, migration, validation and write coordination before directing production writes to it.
3. Shift traffic gradually with a tested rollback/data-compatibility plan; retire old code only after remaining readers and writers have migrated.
4. Repeat until the monolith is small or gone.

## The distributed monolith anti-pattern

The worst outcome is paying all the costs of microservices while getting none of the benefits. Signs you've built a **distributed monolith**:

- **Lockstep deploys**: you can't release service A without releasing B and C at the same time.
- **Shared database**: several services read and write the same tables, so a schema change needs every team.
- **Chatty synchronous chains**: one user request triggers a long chain of blocking calls; if any service is down, everything is.
- **Shared domain libraries**: a "common models" package that every service must upgrade together.

> [!warning] The shared database trap
> Two services writing the same table share a data contract and can become tightly coupled; sharing does not literally make their processes one service. Each service should own its data and expose it only through its API or events. Other services that need the data keep their own copy, updated by events.

The fix is usually to **merge** tightly coupled services back together, or to redraw boundaries so each service owns a complete capability and its data. Several companies have publicly consolidated over-split microservices. Segment wrote in 2018 about merging over 140 near-identical destination services back into a single service, after which deploys took minutes, test suites ran far faster and engineers spent less time on operational toil.

> [!example] A sensible middle path
> A 30-engineer startup runs a modular monolith with modules for accounts, orders and notifications, each with its own schema. Notifications needs to send 2 million emails in a burst and is extracted first, consuming `OrderPlaced` events from a queue. Everything else stays in the monolith until there's a reason to move it.

## Key takeaways
- Strangler fig extraction moves one capability at a time behind a routing or interface boundary.
- Break direct data dependencies, coordinate migration and validate rollback before shifting production writes.
- Lockstep releases, shared tables and chatty required chains reveal coupling that service count cannot fix.
- Merge tightly coupled services or redraw ownership rather than preserving a distributed monolith.

## Further reading
- [Martin Fowler: Strangler Fig Application](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/StranglerFigApplication.html)
- [Segment: Goodbye Microservices](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/developers/best-practices/goodbye-microservices)

questions.prompt: Which of these are warning signs of a **distributed monolith**? Select all that apply.

options.text: Releasing the Orders service requires also releasing Inventory and Billing at the same time.
options.explanation: Correct. Lockstep deploys mean the services are not independently deployable, which removes the main benefit of splitting them.

options.text: Several services read and write the same `customers` table directly.
options.explanation: Correct as a warning sign: direct shared-table access couples data contracts. Backward-compatible changes may not require every team to release together.

options.text: Each service publishes domain events that other services consume asynchronously.
options.explanation: Asynchronous events alone are not evidence of a distributed monolith. They decouple immediate execution, but consumers still depend on schema semantics, delivery and capacity.

options.text: Every service depends on a shared `common-models` library that must be upgraded everywhere at once.
options.explanation: Correct. A shared domain model library forces coordinated upgrades and leaks one team's model into everyone's code.

options.text: Services scale independently, with different instance counts.
options.explanation: Wrong. Independent scaling is a benefit of a genuine microservice split, not a symptom of a distributed monolith.

questions.workedExample:
1. Define the anti-pattern: services that are *physically* separate but *logically* coupled.
2. Check each option for coupling:
   - Lockstep deploys: coupled at release time. Sign.
   - Shared table: coupled at the data level. Sign.
   - Async events: can decouple execution time, but still require compatible schemas and reliable delivery.
   - Shared model library: coupled at build time. Sign.
   - Independent scaling: healthy.
3. Answer: options 0, 1 and 3.

questions.prompt: You're extracting Billing from a monolith with the strangler fig pattern. Billing's tables are also read by the monolith's reporting code via SQL joins. What's the safest sequence?

options.text: Move the billing tables to the new service's database first, then fix whatever breaks in reporting.
options.explanation: Wrong. Moving data first breaks every direct SQL reader at once with no fallback. It's a big-bang change disguised as an incremental one.

options.text: Leave billing tables shared permanently so both the service and the monolith can read and write them.
options.explanation: Wrong. Permanent shared writable tables are the shared-database anti-pattern: the new service is not independently changeable, so you've built a distributed monolith.

options.text: Route all traffic to the new Billing service on day one and delete the monolith's billing code immediately.
options.explanation: Wrong. This removes the ability to roll back and skips the step of migrating the other readers, so reporting breaks.

options.text: Put a routing layer in front, replace reporting's direct joins with calls to a billing interface, build the service behind that interface, migrate data, then route traffic and delete old code.
options.explanation: Correct. Decoupling the readers first means the data can move without breaking them, and the routing layer lets you shift and roll back traffic gradually.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify every coupling to billing data: the HTTP endpoints *and* the SQL joins from reporting.
2. Step 1: add a routing layer (gateway) so `/billing/*` can be redirected later.
3. Step 2: inside the monolith, replace direct joins with calls to a billing interface (or a read model fed by billing events). Now only billing code touches billing tables.
4. Step 3: build the Billing service implementing the same interface.
5. Step 4: migrate and verify data using a consistent snapshot plus change capture or another coordinated protocol. Independent dual writes can diverge; establish one authoritative write path and reconcile catch-up.
6. Step 5: shift traffic gradually (1% → 10% → 100%), with rollback tested against the data written by the new service.
7. Step 6: retire old code and tables only once rollback, retention and remaining-consumer requirements permit it.
8. Rule of thumb: *break the data coupling before you move the data.*

questions.prompt: A director proposes a two-year big-bang rewrite of a 10-year-old monolith into microservices, with the old system frozen until cut-over. Why do experienced engineers usually push for the strangler fig approach instead?

options.text: Strangler fig is faster to complete overall.
options.explanation: Wrong. Incremental migration often takes as long or longer in total. Its value is reducing risk, not total time.

options.text: Big-bang rewrites aren't technically possible for systems over 10 years old.
options.explanation: Wrong. They're possible; they're just very risky.

options.text: Strangler fig delivers value and feedback per extracted capability, keeps the old system running as a fallback, and avoids a long freeze where the rewrite chases a moving target.
options.explanation: Correct. Incremental migration creates smaller feedback loops. Routing rollback is safe only while old and new behavior and data remain compatible.

options.text: Strangler fig avoids having to migrate any data.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each extracted capability still needs its data migrated. Strangler fig just does it one capability at a time.

questions.workedExample:
1. Big-bang risks: years without user value; business needs change during the freeze; the old system's undocumented behaviour is only discovered at cut-over; one huge risky switch.
2. Strangler fig: router in front → extract one capability → coordinate/migrate its data → shift traffic gradually (1%,10%,100%) → retire old code after validation.
3. A route change alone cannot undo incompatible writes; plan data compatibility, reconciliation and rollback before migration.
4. Total time may be similar, but risk is spread over many small steps.

lessons.title: Making application instances replaceable
lessons.summary: Decide which state must survive outside an application instance and which working state can be rebuilt.
lessons.body:
A common way to scale an application tier is **adding instances behind a load balancer**. Making requests independent of any particular instance simplifies this; stateful systems can also scale through partitioning or replication. That property is called being **stateless**, and most large web architectures are built around it.

## What "stateless" really means

A stateless application tier does not rely on **instance-local client state surviving until a later request**. Rebuildable caches and per-request working memory are compatible with this design. Everything a request needs either arrives with the request or is fetched from a shared store.

```
          +---------------+
 users -->| load balancer |
          +--+----+----+--+
             |    |    |
           [A]  [B]  [C]   app servers
             \    |    /    (no local state)
          +---+---+---+---+
          | Redis  |  DB  |  shared state
          +--------+------+
```

It does **not** mean the system has no state. The state has been pushed down into a tier that's designed to hold it (a database, a cache cluster, object storage), so the app tier becomes disposable.

What you get from that:

- **Horizontal scaling.** More instances can increase capacity when requests distribute well and shared dependencies have headroom; scaling is not automatically linear.
- **Easy failure handling.** If server B dies, the load balancer stops sending it traffic. Durable external state remains available under its own guarantees, but in-flight requests, connections and uncommitted work can be lost.
- **Simple deploys.** Rolling updates replace servers one by one; no user is pinned to an old box.
- **Autoscaling.** Servers can be added and removed automatically because none of them is special.

The Twelve-Factor App calls this "execute the app as one or more stateless processes": anything that must persist goes into a backing service.

### Check the replacement boundary

Ask whether another instance could reconstruct everything needed for the next request. A configuration cache fetched again from its source passes that test. A basket or avatar held only in one instance does not. A WebSocket connection necessarily has live connection state, but reconnecting clients need a way to restore room membership and resume useful work on a different instance. Moving state elsewhere also transfers responsibility: persistence, availability and access control belong to the backing service's design.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Any library desk
> A library keeps reservations in a shared catalogue, so a reader can collect a book through any staffed desk.
>
> **How it maps:** Replaceable app instances are the desks; durable session or business records live outside one instance, so another instance can continue serving the reader.
>
> **Where it stops:** The shared store still has failure and consistency requirements. Working memory and local caches are allowed when losing them does not lose required state.

## Key takeaways
- Statelessness removes dependence on durable instance-local client state between requests.
- Shared stores retain durable state; caches and per-request memory can remain local when rebuildable.
- Instance replacement can still lose in-flight work, and shared dependencies still bound scaling.

## Further reading
- [The Twelve-Factor App: Processes](https://12factor.net/processes)

questions.prompt: What makes an application server **stateless**?

options.text: It never reads from or writes to a database.
options.explanation: Wrong. Stateless servers read and write databases all the time. Statelessness is about not keeping client-specific state *locally* between requests.

options.text: It does not depend on instance-local client state being retained between requests, so a replacement instance can reconstruct what it needs
options.explanation: Correct. The state lives in shared backing services, which is what makes instances interchangeable and disposable.

options.text: It runs inside a container.
options.explanation: Wrong. Containers make packaging easy, but a containerised app can still store sessions in memory and be stateful.

options.text: It uses HTTP, which is a stateless protocol.
options.explanation: Wrong. HTTP being stateless at the protocol level says nothing about whether your server keeps sessions or files locally.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: if this request went to a different instance, would it still work?
2. If the session or uploaded file lives only on server A, the answer is no, so A is stateful.
3. If the session is in Redis and files are in S3, any instance can serve it, so the server is stateless.
4. Note that the *system* still has state. It has just been moved to a tier designed to hold it.

questions.prompt: Which of these break the assumption that any app instance can serve any request? Select all that apply.

options.text: Saving user-uploaded avatars to the instance's local disk.
options.explanation: Correct. Other instances can't see that disk, so a later request for the avatar fails unless it hits the same server.

options.text: Keeping a per-process cache of rarely changing config, reloaded every minute.
options.explanation: A rebuildable cache can fit a stateless tier if its freshness and consistency satisfy the request contract. Stale authorization or configuration can still cause correctness problems.

options.text: Storing session data in an in-process hash map.
options.explanation: Correct. Session data in one process's memory ties the user to that process.

options.text: Storing session data in a Redis cluster shared by all instances.
options.explanation: Wrong. A shared store is exactly how you keep instances stateless; any instance can fetch the session.

options.text: Holding a WebSocket connection with an in-memory record of which chat rooms the user joined, with no way to rebuild it.
options.explanation: Correct. If that instance dies, the subscription state is lost. Store subscriptions in a shared store or let the client re-subscribe on reconnect.

questions.workedExample:
1. Test each item: *if this instance vanished, could another one serve the next request correctly?*
2. Local disk avatar: no, file is gone. Breaks it.
3. Config cache: yes, rebuildable from source. Fine.
4. In-process sessions: no. Breaks it.
5. Redis sessions: yes. Fine.
6. WebSocket room membership held only in memory: no, unless rebuilt on reconnect. Breaks it.
7. Answer: 0, 2 and 4.

lessons.title: Choosing where sessions live
lessons.summary: Compare sticky sessions, a shared store and signed tokens under replacement and token revocation.
lessons.body:
Instances are replaceable only when later requests can recover their client state. Choose a session design by both lookup cost and the access cut-off your product needs.

## Where session state goes

Users still log in and have shopping baskets. There are three common places for that state.

### 1. Sticky sessions (avoid as the main strategy)

The load balancer pins each user to one server (via a cookie or IP hash), and the session lives in that server's memory.

- Load spreads unevenly: a few heavy users can overload one box.
- When the server dies or is redeployed, its users lose their sessions.
- Scaling in is painful because you have to drain long-lived sessions.

Sticky sessions are sometimes used as a *performance optimisation* (to keep a warm local cache) on top of a design that still works without them.

### 2. A shared session store

The server stores a random session ID in a cookie, and the session data in Redis or Memcached keyed by that ID.

- Any server can serve any request with a lookup whose latency depends on topology, load and the store.
- The session store must itself be highly available (Redis with replicas, or a managed service).
- Deleting the session prevents future authorizations only once all relevant checks observe the deletion; caches, replicas, failover and already-authorized requests affect cut-off.

### 3. Client-side tokens

The state goes into a signed token the client sends with every request, such as a JWT or a signed cookie.

- Verification can be local if the server already has trusted keys and policy. Signature checking must be accompanied by issuer, audience, expiry and application-specific authorization checks.
- Tokens can't easily be revoked before they expire, so keep them short-lived (say 15 minutes) with a refresh token.
- Every request carries the token, so keep it small (a few hundred bytes, not your whole basket).

| Approach | Lookup cost | Token revocation | Failure risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sticky | none | easy | lose sessions |
| Redis store | Store lookup | Depends on observation/consistency | Store outage or lost state |
| JWT | verify sig | hard | key leak |

> [!tip] Files are state too
> Uploaded files written to `/tmp` on one server are invisible to the others. Send uploads straight to object storage (S3, GCS) instead, ideally via presigned URLs so they don't pass through the app tier at all.

### Token lifecycle checks

With asymmetrically signed access tokens, application servers verify using trusted public keys; protect the private signing key and plan rotation. Revoke refresh tokens in a server-side store when disabling future renewal. Already-issued access tokens remain usable until their expiry unless each authorisation performs an enforced token revocation check. Rotate refresh tokens on use and detect reuse atomically. Reuse may indicate theft or legitimate concurrent requests; invalidating a refresh-token family stops further renewal once enforced, but does not itself invalidate already-issued access tokens. A short access-token lifetime is a design example, not a universal security optimum; validation, key distribution and clock tolerance are part of the policy.

## Key takeaways
- Sticky sessions lose instance-local sessions when their instance disappears; use them only where the design still works without affinity.
- A shared session store permits replacement but makes authorisation depend on observing the current session policy.
- JWT signature checks require issuer, audience, expiry and authorisation checks; expiry limits exposure rather than providing immediate token revocation.

## Further reading
- [The Twelve-Factor App: Processes](https://12factor.net/processes)
- [OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html)

questions.prompt: An e-commerce site stores shopping baskets in each app server's memory and uses sticky sessions. During a deploy, servers are restarted one at a time. What do users experience?

options.text: Nothing, because the load balancer copies sessions to the new server.
options.explanation: Wrong. A load balancer routes traffic; it doesn't replicate in-memory application state between servers.

options.text: Users pinned to each restarted server lose their baskets and may be logged out.
options.explanation: Correct. With in-memory sessions, the state dies with the process. Sticky routing then sends those users to a new server that has never seen them.

options.text: All users across all servers lose their baskets at once.
options.explanation: Wrong. Only users pinned to the restarted server are affected each time, though over a full rolling deploy that ends up being everyone.

options.text: Users are unaffected because sticky sessions store the basket in the cookie.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sticky sessions only store a routing hint in the cookie (which server to use), not the basket data.

questions.workedExample:
1. Where does the basket live? In server A's RAM.
2. Deploy restarts A, so the RAM is wiped.
3. Users stuck to A are now routed elsewhere with no session data.
4. Over the whole rolling deploy, every server restarts, so eventually every user loses their basket once.
5. Fix: store sessions in Redis (or a signed token) so restarts don't matter.

questions.prompt: Your API uses JWT access tokens valid for 24 hours. A user reports their laptop was stolen, and you need to cut off access immediately. What's the core problem, and what's the standard mitigation?

options.text: JWTs are encrypted, so they can't be read; nothing more is needed.
options.explanation: Most JWTs are signed rather than encrypted. A stolen bearer token may remain accepted while its expiry and validation policy allow; signature validity alone does not prove the presenter is its owner.

options.text: Rotate the signing key; this is the normal way to revoke one user.
options.explanation: A key rotation only invalidates old tokens once every verifier stops accepting the old key. It is broad rather than per-user token revocation, and cached keys or overlap can delay cut-off.

options.text: Self-contained tokens can't be revoked before expiry without a server-side check; use short-lived access tokens (for example 15 minutes) with revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist for emergencies.
options.explanation: Correct as a design approach. Token revocation for refresh credentials prevents future refresh once observed, but existing access tokens continue until expiry or a separate enforced token revocation check.

options.text: Delete the user's session from Redis.
options.explanation: Wrong. A pure JWT design has no server-side session to delete; that's the trade-off you made to avoid the lookup.

questions.workedExample:
1. Why JWTs scale: any server can verify the signature with no shared lookup.
2. The cost: the server has no record to delete, so the token stays valid until `exp`.
3. With a 24 h lifetime, a stolen token works for up to 24 h.
4. Mitigation:
   - Access token lifetime 15 min.
   - Refresh token stored server-side, revoked on 'log out everywhere'.
   - After refresh is disabled, existing 15-minute access tokens can remain usable until expiry (plus configured clock tolerance); merely changing the policy does not shorten already-issued 24-hour tokens.
5. For prompt cut-off, require every authorization to consult a consistently enforced denylist of revoked token IDs in Redis, accepting a lookup on each request.

questions.prompt: Your login service issues 15-minute JWT access tokens and 30-day refresh tokens. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply. Assume asymmetrically signed access tokens and a validated issuer/audience/expiry policy.

options.text: Keep refresh tokens in a server-side store so they can be revoked, and check it whenever a refresh is attempted.
options.explanation: Correct. A server-side refresh-session record (often storing a token hash rather than raw token) supports token revocation checks at refresh. Refresh frequency depends on client activity and policy.

options.text: Put the user's full profile and basket in the access token so no service needs to look anything up.
options.explanation: Wrong. Tokens travel on every request; a bloated token costs bandwidth, may exceed header limits, and the data inside goes stale.

options.text: Rotate refresh tokens on each use and treat reuse of an old one as a sign of theft.
options.explanation: Correct. Reuse detection is evidence of replay, though legitimate concurrent clients can also reuse a token. Family invalidation must be atomic and does not automatically revoke issued access tokens.

options.text: Let any app server verify access tokens with the public key, without calling the auth service.
options.explanation: Correct with trusted key distribution and the stated validation policy. Signature validity alone is insufficient; enforce issuer, audience, expiry and required claims.

options.text: Make access tokens valid for 30 days so users don't need refresh tokens.
options.explanation: Wrong. A long-lived bearer token that can't be revoked is a 30-day window for anyone who steals it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Access token: short-lived, small, verified locally with the public key.
2. Refresh token: long-lived, stored server-side, revocable.
3. After token revocation for refresh credentials is enforced, already-issued access tokens can remain usable for their remaining lifetime plus allowed clock tolerance; stronger cut-off needs additional checks.
4. Rotation: each refresh returns a new refresh token; presenting an already-used one revokes the family.
5. Refresh lookup frequency depends on active clients and their refresh schedules; it is not exactly one lookup per user per 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Scaling ahead of shared bottlenecks
lessons.summary: Choose scaling signals, allow for readiness delay and budget database connections as instances grow.
lessons.body:
Replacement makes automatic scaling possible, but it does not make capacity arrive immediately. The goal is to keep admitted work within every tier's sustainable capacity.

## Autoscaling

With stateless servers you can let a controller adjust the count to match load. Typical signals:

- **CPU utilisation**: simple and widely used; choose a target from load testing and required headroom; 50–70% is an illustrative starting range, not a universal optimum.
- **Requests per second per instance**: better when the work is I/O-bound and CPU stays low.
- **Queue depth**: for workers, scale on the number of messages waiting.
- **Schedules**: scale up before a known peak (9 am logins, a 7 pm TV advert).

Autoscaling isn't instant. VM provisioning, image pulls and application warm-up all take time; measure readiness time for the actual workload rather than assuming a VM/container timing range. If traffic can double in 30 seconds, autoscaling alone won't save you. Keep a baseline buffer, use predictive or scheduled scaling, and shed load gracefully.

> [!warning] Scaling the web tier can break the database
> Going from 10 to 100 app servers, each with a pool of 20 database connections, takes you from 200 to 2,000 connections. Whether that exceeds limits or sustainable load depends on database configuration, memory and active query demand. Use a connection pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) and remember the bottleneck usually moves down a tier.

More app instances can exhaust the shared database connection budget even when each instance has a small pool. The example assumes every pool is full. A pooler such as PgBouncer can let many client connections share fewer database connections, subject to the pooling mode and transaction workload.

## Containers

A **container** packages an application and its dependencies into an image for a supported platform; host kernel, architecture, configuration and external services still affect behavior. Unlike a VM, it shares the host's kernel, which can reduce some virtualization overhead. Time to serving readiness still depends on the runtime, image availability, initialization and dependencies.

Containers suit stateless services: an image is immutable, any copy is interchangeable, and you replace them rather than patch them.

## Key takeaways
- Use metrics that represent the actual bottleneck and keep capacity ready before predictable bursts.
- An instance count multiplied by its full pool size bounds requested database connections.
- Containers package dependencies but readiness still depends on images, initialisation and backing services.
- Pool connections and bound or shed excess work before autoscaling moves overload into another tier.

## Further reading
- [Kubernetes: Overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/)

questions.prompt: A flash sale doubles traffic in 20 seconds. Your web tier autoscales on CPU and new VMs take about 3 minutes to boot and pass health checks. Error rates spike for 3 minutes, and then the database falls over as the new instances come online. What's the best set of changes?

options.text: Lower the CPU target from 60% to 30% and change nothing else.
options.explanation: Wrong. A lower target adds headroom, which helps the first spike, but the 3-minute boot time is unchanged and the database connection storm is not addressed at all.

options.text: Pre-scale on a schedule before the sale, switch to faster-starting containers on warm nodes, put a connection pooler in front of the database, and shed or queue excess load.
options.explanation: These changes address provisioning delay and connection pressure; validate readiness time and query capacity rather than assuming containers and a pooler guarantee recovery.

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions so each user stays on one server.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sticky sessions don't add capacity or speed up scaling, and they make load distribution worse during a spike.

options.text: Remove autoscaling and permanently run 10× the normal capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's very expensive, and the database still faces 10× the connections. It treats the symptom rather than the bottlenecks.

questions.workedExample:
1. A flash-sale arrival spike can happen faster than new pods become useful.
2. Image pulls, scheduling, startup and readiness all take time.
3. Pre-scale for predictable demand and apply admission control or queues within the product’s latency budget.
4. Check shared database capacity as well as the app tier.

questions.prompt: Autoscaling adds many app pods during a traffic spike. Each keeps its old database connection-pool limit. The database rejects connections while app CPU is modest. What is the most direct explanation and response?

options.text: Increase every pod’s pool limit so rejected connections succeed.
options.explanation: That increases attempted connections and can worsen the shared bottleneck.

options.text: Ignore the errors until autoscaling finishes; more pods necessarily solve them.
options.explanation: More clients may increase the pressure even after rollout completes.

options.text: The combined pool demand can exceed the shared database limit; budget connections across replicas and use suitable pooling or admission control.
options.explanation: Correct. Scaling clients does not scale the database connection budget.

options.text: Low app CPU proves that the service has spare capacity everywhere.
options.explanation: Requests can be blocked on I/O while CPU stays low.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the constrained shared resource: accepted database connections.
2. More pods create more potential pools against that same resource.
3. Bound total connections, queue or shed work, and consider a compatible connection pooler.
4. Measure database capacity before expanding the budget.

lessons.title: Keeping traffic safe during pod replacement
lessons.summary: Connect Kubernetes routing, probes, rollout limits and graceful shutdown to instance replacement.
lessons.body:
The earlier units made instances disposable and identified capacity limits. Kubernetes must now replace those instances while routing traffic and finishing work safely.

## Kubernetes basics

Running hundreds of containers by hand isn't feasible. **Kubernetes** is an orchestrator: you declare the state you want, and its controllers continuously work to make reality match.

The core objects:

- **Pod**: the smallest unit, one or more containers that share a network namespace and are scheduled together.
- **Kubernetes Deployment**: "keep 10 replicas of this pod template running"; it handles rolling updates and rollbacks.
- **Service**: a normal ClusterIP Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name for matching endpoints. Headless and ExternalName Services behave differently.
- **Ingress / Gateway**: routes external HTTP traffic to Services.
- **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**: adjusts a Kubernetes Deployment's replica count from metrics such as CPU.
- **Probes**: readiness contributes to endpoint eligibility for normal Service traffic; a liveness failure reaching its threshold can restart the failing container under its restart policy.

```
 Ingress
    |
 Service "web"  (stable DNS)
    |
 +--+-----+------+
 |        |      |
Pod      Pod    Pod   <- Deployment
                         replicas: 3
                       <- HPA: 3..20
```

> [!example] A rolling deploy
> A Kubernetes Deployment has 10 replicas with `maxUnavailable: 1` and `maxSurge: 2`. The controller allows up to 2 extra non-terminating pods and can reduce available capacity to 9 during normal rollout; it need not wait for both new pods before removing any old pod. Terminating pods can temporarily make the total higher. This aims to maintain availability, but statelessness and schema compatibility alone do not guarantee invisible updates: APIs, sessions, capacity and draining must also remain compatible.

## Graceful shutdown

Stateless doesn't mean you can kill a pod mid-request. When Kubernetes terminates a pod, two paths proceed **in parallel**: the kubelet runs any `preStop` hook and then sends the stop signal (normally `SIGTERM`), while the control plane marks the terminating endpoint not ready for normal Service traffic. Load balancers and every node's kube-proxy take a moment to notice that removal, so new requests can keep arriving during the propagation delay, including after SIGTERM; there is no universal one- or two-second bound.

A well-behaved server therefore:

1. Keeps serving while termination begins and endpoint readiness changes propagate. A `preStop` hook may provide a short delay **before** `SIGTERM`; the hook and subsequent draining share the termination grace period.
2. Stops accepting new connections and fails its readiness probe.
3. Finishes in-flight requests, within the grace period (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, 30 s by default, after which it gets `SIGKILL`).
4. Exits.

A server that exits the instant it receives `SIGTERM` drops the requests that were still on their way to it, which shows up as a handful of connection resets on every deploy.

Long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming) need extra care: clients must be able to reconnect to another instance and resume.

## Key takeaways
- A normal Service routes to eligible endpoints while a Kubernetes Deployment replaces pod replicas.
- Readiness controls normal traffic eligibility; a liveness failure can restart the container.
- Rolling-update limits allow surplus and unavailable capacity within configured bounds.
- Endpoint changes and shutdown proceed concurrently: allow propagation and drain in-flight work within the grace period.

## Further reading
- [Kubernetes: Overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/)
- [Kubernetes: Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)
- [Kubernetes: Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

questions.prompt: During every Kubernetes rolling deploy, a small number of clients get connection-reset errors, even though readiness probes are configured. Which explanation and fix is most likely right?

options.text: Pods exit immediately on SIGTERM while in-flight requests are running, and endpoint removal is still propagating; handle SIGTERM by draining in-flight requests (and optionally a short preStop delay) before exiting.
options.explanation: Correct as a likely cause. Endpoint updates and local termination proceed concurrently; preStop runs before the stop signal and shares the grace-period budget. Draining reduces this failure mode but must be validated.

options.text: The liveness probe is too slow; make it run every second.
options.explanation: Wrong. Liveness probes decide when to restart unhealthy pods. They have nothing to do with how a pod is shut down during a deploy.

options.text: Rolling deploys always drop some requests; switch to deleting all pods and recreating them.
options.explanation: Deleting every pod removes serving capacity. A rolling update with validated draining and sufficient capacity reduces these connection-reset failures; it does not guarantee every request succeeds.

options.text: The Kubernetes Deployment has too many replicas; reduce it to one.
options.explanation: A single replica is fragile, but a rolling update with surge capacity can overlap old and new pods; one replica does not by itself imply every deployment has downtime.

questions.workedExample:
1. Termination starts concurrent endpoint updates and kubelet shutdown. Normal terminating endpoints become not ready; propagation is not instantaneous.
2. The kubelet runs any preStop hook before sending the configured stop signal (normally SIGTERM). Both hook and draining consume the grace period.
3. An app exiting immediately can drop routed or in-flight work.
4. Measure propagation, continue serving during an appropriate preStop delay, then stop accepting new work and drain with a bounded deadline. Reconnect long-lived clients.
5. Load-test rollouts and failure paths. This reduces avoidable resets but does not guarantee zero errors under every failure.

questions.prompt: For an ordinary Kubernetes Deployment using normal Service endpoint routing, what is the difference when a readiness or liveness probe reaches its configured failure threshold?

options.text: Readiness failure restarts the container; liveness failure removes it from the Service.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's the other way round.

options.text: Both restart the container; liveness just checks more often.
options.explanation: Wrong. Only a liveness failure triggers a restart. Readiness controls traffic.

options.text: Readiness failure only logs a warning; liveness failure deletes the Kubernetes Deployment.
options.explanation: Wrong. Neither deletes the Kubernetes Deployment. Readiness takes the pod out of rotation; liveness restarts it.

options.text: Readiness failure removes normal endpoint eligibility without itself restarting the container; liveness failure can cause its restart under the configured policy
options.explanation: Correct. Readiness answers 'should traffic come here now?'; liveness answers 'is this process stuck and in need of a restart?'

questions.workedExample:
1. Pod warming its cache at startup: not ready yet, but not broken. Readiness fails, so it gets no traffic. No restart.
2. Pod deadlocked: liveness fails, so the kubelet restarts it.
3. Common mistake: making liveness check the database. If the DB blips, every pod restarts at once and makes the outage worse.
4. Rolling update behavior uses availability and maxUnavailable/maxSurge settings; it need not wait for every new pod before removing any old pod.

link.title: Kubernetes: Liveness, readiness and startup probes

questions.prompt: A healthy Kubernetes Deployment has 10 replicas, maxSurge: 2 and maxUnavailable: 0. What limits does the rolling-update controller aim to maintain, excluding independent failures and allowing terminating pods to finish?

options.text: Up to 12 non-terminating pods and at least 10 available pods under normal rollout control; total existing pods can be higher while termination finishes
options.explanation: Correct. Surge and unavailability constrain rollout decisions; terminating pods can temporarily consume extra resources, and node/app failures can still reduce actual availability.

options.text: At most 10 pods exist, and at least 8 are ready.
options.explanation: Wrong. That describes maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 2.

options.text: At most 20 pods exist, because all new pods start before any old one stops.
options.explanation: Wrong. That would be a blue-green style switch. maxSurge caps extras at 2.

options.text: At most 12 pods exist, and the number of ready pods may drop to 0 briefly.
options.explanation: The controller does not intentionally remove all available capacity with maxUnavailable: 0. It does not provide an unconditional minimum under failures or an absolute total-pod cap.

questions.workedExample:
1. Desired count: 10.
2. Surge allowance: 2 additional non-terminating pods during normal rollout.
3. maxUnavailable: 0 directs the controller to retain desired available capacity as it replaces pods.
4. Availability can differ from readiness when minReadySeconds applies.
5. Terminating old pods can remain present and consume resources beyond the nominal 12 until their grace periods end.
6. These are controller policies, not a promise against node outages, probe failures, insufficient capacity or incompatible versions.

lessons.title: Reading and stabilising HPA recommendations
lessons.summary: Explain HPA recommendations and why readiness, tolerance and stabilisation affect actual capacity.
lessons.body:
A Kubernetes Deployment sets a desired replica count. Its HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts that count from observed metrics; a recommendation still needs scheduled, ready pods before it becomes usable capacity.

## HPA replica recommendations

For a CPU utilisation target, percentages are relative to configured CPU requests, not a node's total capacity. The HPA's job is to pick a pod count that would bring the average metric back to the target. If 4 pods average 90% CPU and you want 60%, the same total work spread over more pods brings each one down. The simplified rule from the Kubernetes documentation is:

```formula reference
R_new = ⌈R × M / T⌉
where
R_new: the number of pod replicas the HPA will ask for
R: the number of pod replicas running now
M: the current average value of the metric across the pods, e.g. CPU at 90 % of each pod's CPU request
T: the target value you configured for that metric, e.g. 60 %
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number, because you can't run part of a pod
%: per cent of each pod's requested CPU
In words: scale the pod count by how far the metric is above or below target, then round up.
```

For this example, assume equal CPU requests and valid metrics for every pod. Missing metrics and not-yet-ready pods can alter the controller's recommendation.

The rule assumes the load divides evenly across pods and stays the same while new pods start. In practice it is recalculated every few seconds (15 s by default), so the count converges over several steps.

The HPA also ignores small deviations (a default tolerance of about 10%) and, by default, uses the highest recent recommendation within a default 5-minute scale-down stabilisation window, so a brief dip doesn't remove pods you'll need again a minute later.

When the cluster itself runs out of room, a **cluster autoscaler** (or Karpenter, originally built by AWS) can provision nodes when suitable capacity is available and policy permits. Timing is workload/provider-dependent; quotas, capacity shortages and scheduling constraints can leave pods Pending.

## Key takeaways
- CPU utilisation targets use pod CPU requests as the denominator.
- The simplified HPA calculation scales the current count by current metric over target, then rounds up.
- Tolerance and scale-down stabilisation avoid reacting to small or short-lived changes.
- A recommendation is not ready capacity: node availability, quotas and scheduling can delay new pods.

## Further reading
- [Kubernetes: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)

questions.prompt: An HPA observes average CPU utilisation well above its target. Metrics are valid, CPU requests are equal and demand can spread across pods. What should you expect?

options.text: It should request more replicas, but new capacity helps only after pods are scheduled, ready and receive work.
options.explanation: Correct. The proportional recommendation is a desired count, not instant capacity or proof that the shared bottleneck disappeared.

options.text: It should remove replicas to reduce aggregate CPU usage.
options.explanation: Removing pods concentrates the same demand onto fewer workers.

options.text: It guarantees latency will meet its objective immediately.
options.explanation: Scheduling, startup and other bottlenecks can delay or prevent improvement.

options.text: It should change each pod’s CPU request instead of the replica count.
options.explanation: The HPA changes replicas; changing requests is a different control.

questions.workedExample:
1. Above-target utilisation indicates pressure relative to the requested CPU.
2. More ready pods may spread divisible work.
3. Verify readiness, shared dependencies and latency after scaling; the metric is not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Traffic drops for 2 minutes during a TV advert break and then returns. Your HPA has `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0`, and after each break you see a burst of 5xx errors while pods come back. What's the most likely fix?

options.text: Increase the CPU target from 60% to 90% so fewer pods are needed.
options.explanation: Wrong. Higher utilisation means less headroom, making spikes worse, and it doesn't stop the flapping.

options.text: Restore a scale-down stabilisation window (the default is 5 minutes) so the HPA keeps pods through short dips.
options.explanation: Correct. The HPA uses the highest recommendation over the window before scaling down, so a 2-minute dip doesn't remove capacity you need again straight away.

options.text: Switch the HPA to scale on memory instead of CPU.
options.explanation: Wrong. The problem is how quickly it scales down after a dip, not which metric it reads.

options.text: Use sticky sessions so returning users go back to their old pods.
options.explanation: Wrong. Those pods were removed, and sticky sessions don't add capacity.

questions.workedExample:
1. Window 0: dip → scale down at once → traffic returns → pods start again (seconds to minutes) → errors meanwhile.
2. Default 300 s window: the HPA scales down only to the highest replica count recommended in the last 5 minutes.
3. A 2-minute dip following an in-window high recommendation preserves that recommendation; an older high recommendation that has already expired does not provide this protection.
4. Scale-up stays fast (no window by default), so real growth is still handled.
5. Trade-off: you pay for some idle pods for a few minutes.

lessons.title: Finding changing service instances
lessons.summary: Compare registry-aware clients with stable-name routing and diagnose stale discovery caches.
lessons.body:
Once you have more than one service, two questions appear straight away. **How does Orders find a healthy Payments instance** when instances are created and destroyed every few minutes? And **should Orders wait for Payments to answer**, or send a message and move on?

## Why discovery is needed

Hard-coding an instance IP is fragile when instances change. A stable DNS name such as payments.internal:8080 can still be appropriate when discovery or routing updates its backing endpoints. In a cloud or Kubernetes world:

- Instances autoscale up and down.
- Deploys replace every instance with new IP addresses.
- Failed instances are removed and replaced automatically.

So something must keep an up-to-date list of healthy instances (the **service registry**) and something must use that list to pick one for each call.

Instances get into the registry by **self-registration** (the instance registers itself and sends heartbeats, as with Netflix Eureka or Consul agents) or by **third-party registration** (the platform registers them, as Kubernetes does from pod readiness).

## Client-side discovery

The calling service queries the registry and chooses an instance itself.

```
 [Orders]---1. lookup--->[Registry]
    |    <--2. [ip1,ip2,ip3]
    |
    +--3. call ip2--->[Payments #2]
```

- **Pros:** no extra hop; the client can use smart load balancing (least-requests, zone-aware routing, retries to a different instance).
- **Cons:** every language needs a discovery client library, and logic is duplicated across stacks. Netflix's Ribbon + Eureka is the classic example (Ribbon is now in maintenance mode); gRPC's client-side load balancing is a modern one.

## Server-side discovery

The client calls a stable address; a load balancer or router looks up the registry and forwards the request.

```
 [Orders]--call payments-->[ LB / proxy ]
                              |     |
                       [Pay #1]  [Pay #2]
```
