lessons.title: Adding table semantics to lake files
lessons.summary: Compare warehouses, lakes and lakehouses while connecting column pruning and table snapshots to query reliability.
lessons.body:
Batch and stream jobs both need durable inputs and reliable analytical outputs. The file layout and table metadata determine which bytes a query reads and which committed snapshot it observes.

## Data lakes, warehouses and lakehouses

Where does all this data live?

- A **data warehouse** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) provides managed analytical queries, commonly using columnar storage. It can hold raw and semi-structured as well as cleaned data; schema behavior depends on its table and data types. Columnar storage means a query that sums one column out of 200 reads only that column, compressed.
- A **data lake** stores raw files of any type (JSON, CSV, Parquet, images, logs) cheaply in object storage like S3. Schema is applied on read. It's flexible but can become a "data swamp" without cataloguing and quality controls.
- A **lakehouse** adds a **table format** (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi) over data files in the lake, often Parquet (Iceberg also supports Avro and ORC), providing table-level commit/snapshot mechanisms, schema evolution and metadata used by compatible engines. Exact transaction scope and retained time-travel history depend on the format, catalog, engine and configuration, so warehouse-style SQL engines can query lake data reliably.

```
 OLTP DBs --CDC-+
 app events ----+--> [Kafka] -> streams
 3rd party -----+       |
                         v
            [lake: S3 + Iceberg tables]
              raw -> cleaned -> aggregated
                         |
           [SQL engines / warehouse / ML]
```

A common layering is **bronze** (raw), **silver** (cleaned, deduplicated, conformed) and **gold** (business-level aggregates).

> [!note] ETL vs ELT
> Classic **ETL** transforms data *before* loading it into the warehouse. Modern **ELT** loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse or lakehouse with SQL (often with dbt), because storage is cheap and compute is elastic.

## Choosing

- Need results within seconds (fraud, alerting, live dashboards, feature updates)? **Stream.**
- Processing large historical datasets, training models, or results needed daily? **Batch.**
- Both, with one codebase? **Kappa-style streaming plus replay**, or a unified engine.
- Retain sufficient raw data or suitable snapshots for the required rebuild horizon, subject to deletion and retention requirements. Reproducible replay also needs relevant schemas, code and external inputs.

### Reading only the data the query needs

Suppose a table has equal-sized columns and equal daily volumes. A one-column query needs only that column in columnar files; a date-partitioned layout can then exclude unrelated days before reading data. Compression reduces the remaining payload further. These mechanisms can combine, but real queries also read metadata and may need predicate columns, row groups or extra pages. They are not a production benchmark. A table format contributes snapshot and schema rules; it does not automatically guarantee good file sizes, cataloguing or query plans.

## Key takeaways
- Warehouses provide analytical query services; lakes store raw files; lakehouse formats define tables over those files.
- Columnar layout, date partition pruning and compression reduce payload reads under explicit workload assumptions.
- Compatible readers use committed table metadata rather than treating arbitrary file listings as a transaction.
- Retain suitable raw data and reproducibility inputs for the required rebuild horizon.

## Further reading
- [Wikipedia: Data lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lake)
- [Apache Iceberg documentation](https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/)

questions.prompt: A company dumps raw JSON from 40 sources into S3. Analysts complain that queries are slow, nobody knows which files are current, concurrent jobs sometimes see incomplete multi-file table updates, and a schema change broke a dashboard. What's the most appropriate evolution?

options.text: Move everything into the production Postgres database so analysts can use SQL.
options.explanation: Wrong. A row-oriented OLTP database isn't built for scanning terabytes, and analytical queries would compete with production traffic.

options.text: Adopt a lakehouse table format (e.g. Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) over columnar Parquet files, with a catalogue, layered raw/cleaned/aggregated tables, and schema evolution rules.
options.explanation: Columnar files can reduce scan work, and compatible table-format readers use atomic metadata commits for consistent snapshots. Catalog and schema governance remain necessary; this does not fix every slow query.

options.text: Add more JSON files with clearer names.
options.explanation: Wrong. Naming doesn't provide atomic commits, columnar efficiency or schema management. It just makes the swamp slightly better labelled.

options.text: Replace S3 with a larger network file share.
options.explanation: Wrong. The storage medium isn't the problem. The issues are format, transactions and metadata, which a file share doesn't solve either.

questions.workedExample:
1. Map each complaint to a cause:
   - Slow queries: row-based JSON, so every query parses whole files. Columnar Parquet reads only the needed columns, compressed.
   - Which files are current: no table metadata. A table format tracks the exact file list per snapshot.
   - Incomplete table updates: S3 objects are individually atomic, but an arbitrary set of files is not a table transaction. Iceberg/Delta commit a new snapshot atomically; compatible readers see one committed snapshot; bypassing the table metadata loses that guarantee.
   - Schema breakage: no schema governance. Table formats support explicit, compatible schema evolution.
2. Organise as bronze (raw) → silver (cleaned) → gold (aggregates), with SQL engines (Trino, Spark, Snowflake) on top.
3. Result: warehouse-like reliability on cheap object storage.

questions.prompt: Analysts sum one metric for one day from a large event table. Which storage design helps avoid reading unrelated payload while still providing a consistent table snapshot?

options.text: Unpartitioned JSON files with clearer filenames alone.
options.explanation: Names do not provide column pruning or atomic table metadata commits.

options.text: A larger object-store bucket without changing file layout.
options.explanation: More space does not make the query skip irrelevant columns or days.

options.text: Read every object and discard unrelated rows after parsing.
options.explanation: That still incurs the unnecessary input work.

options.text: Columnar files with suitable date pruning, compression and a table format used by compatible readers.
options.explanation: Correct. These address different concerns: columns, date ranges, payload size and committed table metadata.

questions.workedExample:
1. Columnar files let the engine read required columns.
2. Date partition or metadata pruning can skip unrelated data.
3. Compression reduces the remaining payload, while metadata and predicate work remain.
4. A compatible table-format reader chooses one committed snapshot; the format does not automatically fix poor layouts or plans.

lessons.title: Budgeting distance and recovery objectives
lessons.summary: Relate propagation delay, replication acknowledgement and RPO/RTO to a chosen regional failure model.
lessons.body:
A cloud region may offer several availability zones, each with separate infrastructure and possibly multiple data centres. A correctly configured multi-AZ workload can tolerate specified zone failures, but a region label alone does not guarantee application availability. So why go **multi-region**?

- **Disaster recovery**: whole regions do fail, or partially fail in ways that look total (control-plane outages, bad deploys of regional services, major network events).
- **Latency**: long paths impose propagation delay. Light in optical fibre travels at roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, about 200 km every millisecond, so distance alone sets a minimum delay (illustrated below). Serving Australian users from Australia matters.
- **Data residency**: laws and contracts may require data about EU residents, or a particular government's citizens, to stay in specific places.

The minimum one-way delay over a fibre path is just distance divided by speed:

Distance imposes a minimum travel time before processing or queuing. A hypothetical 17,000 km fibre path takes about 85 ms one way at the stated speed, with a round trip taking at least 170 ms.

This is a floor, not a prediction: real routes are longer than the straight line, and routers and queues add more. Measure actual round-trip times (RTTs).

It's also expensive and hard. Extra regions add infrastructure and operating costs and, more importantly, force you to confront **the speed of light in your data layer**.

## The fundamental trade-off

Synchronous acknowledgment latency depends on required replicas, distance, storage and protocol. Benchmark the chosen deployment.

That gives you a choice for each piece of data:

- **Synchronous cross-region replication**: can protect acknowledged commits from loss of one region when they are durably retained in a surviving region and failover selects the correct replica; this can meet a zero-loss objective for that failure model. Each required remote acknowledgment adds latency, and writes stop if the required remote acknowledgements or quorum become unreachable; a three-region quorum can continue after losing one region.
- **Asynchronous replication**: fast local writes, but a failure can lose acknowledged writes not yet durably replicated. Observed lag does not by itself guarantee a worst-case recovery point.

This is CAP and PACELC in practice: under a partition you choose consistency or availability, and even without one you choose latency or consistency.

Two numbers frame every DR design:

- **RPO** (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): how long you can be down.

## Key takeaways
- Distance creates a propagation floor; measured RTT includes routes, equipment and queues.
- Synchronous remote durability can protect acknowledged writes for a defined region-loss model at a coordination cost.
- Asynchronous replication risks unreplicated acknowledged writes; observed lag is not a worst-case loss bound.
- RPO targets allowable loss and RTO targets restoration time; validate both with recovery evidence.

## Further reading
- [AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html)
- [Azure Architecture Center: Geode pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/geodes)

questions.prompt: A company's RPO is 5 minutes and RTO is 1 hour. What does that mean?

options.text: They can lose at most 5 minutes of data and must be back up within 1 hour of a disaster.
options.explanation: These are recovery objectives, not proof that the deployed system can meet them. Validate recovery point and duration in the relevant failure scenarios.

options.text: They can be down for at most 5 minutes and lose at most 1 hour of data.
options.explanation: Wrong. This swaps the two. RPO is about data loss (the point you recover *to*); RTO is about time to recover.

options.text: Backups run every hour and take 5 minutes.
options.explanation: Wrong. RPO and RTO are objectives, not backup schedules. Hourly backups alone might leave roughly an hour of changes uncovered; retained logs can support a much newer recovery point. Backup cadence does not by itself determine achieved recovery.

options.text: Replication lag must always be exactly 5 minutes.
options.explanation: Wrong. RPO is a maximum tolerable loss. Normal replication lag should be well below it.

questions.workedExample:
1. A five-minute RPO is the target maximum loss window; test that backups/logs or surviving replicas can provide it. A five-minute backup schedule alone is not proof.
2. A one-hour RTO is the target restoration time; include detection, decisions, provisioning, restore, validation and routing.
3. Stricter objectives may require durable synchronous replication and ready capacity, but do not uniquely require active-active.

questions.prompt: A UK-based service has growing numbers of users in Australia, who complain about slowness. Each page makes 4 sequential API round trips to London (about 280 ms each). What's the main benefit of serving them from an Australian region? Treat 280 ms as the measured existing RTT and assume the proposed local path measures 20 ms and does not call London synchronously.

options.text: It removes much of the waiting on the measured long remote paths, provided requests do not synchronously return to London.
options.explanation: Correct. A nearby measured serving path shortens the sequential network waits; the whole dependency path must benefit.

options.text: It makes the London servers' CPUs faster.
options.explanation: Moving the serving location changes the network path, not the speed of London’s processors.

options.text: Nothing; the speed of light is fast enough that distance doesn't matter.
options.explanation: Distance creates a propagation floor and the prompt supplies measurements showing a large path difference.

options.text: It guarantees strong consistency with London.
options.explanation: Regional placement alone does not define replication or transaction consistency. Remote coordination and asynchronous visibility have separate trade-offs.

1. The question supplies measured remote and local path times.
2. Serial network trips accumulate, so a nearby serving path can remove much of that waiting.
3. A synchronous call back to London can reintroduce the long path.

options.text: A successful local disk write is enough to acknowledge when Virginia is unreachable.
options.explanation: Doing so changes the stated durability policy.

options.text: Commits wait for remote acknowledgement; the surviving durable copy can protect acknowledged data after London is lost, but an unreachable Virginia can stop writes.
options.explanation: Correct. Failover must select the durable copy and fence the old writer; asynchronous fallback changes the loss guarantee.

options.text: Strong replication automatically makes every failover instantaneous and correct.
options.explanation: Detection, fencing, routing, capacity and recovery validation remain necessary.

2. That adds remote coordination to each commit’s critical path.

lessons.title: Preparing standby failover and good backups
lessons.summary: Compare standby warmth and exercise restore paths that replication alone cannot provide.
lessons.body:
The previous unit set recovery objectives. Active-passive keeps one authoritative serving region and prepares a standby; a successful restore must also survive logical mistakes.

## Active-passive

One region (primary) serves all traffic; another (standby) receives replicated data and takes over if the primary fails.

```
        users
          |
     [ DNS / GLB ]
       |       :  (failover)
       v       v
  [Region A]  [Region B]
   active      standby
     DB ==async==> DB replica
```

Variants by how "warm" the standby is (AWS names these in its DR guidance):

| Strategy | Standby | Recovery work |
|---|---|---|
| Backup & restore | Backups | Restore data and provision services |
| Pilot light | Data and core infrastructure | Start missing services and scale |
| Warm standby | Reduced working deployment | Redirect traffic and add capacity |
| Hot standby | Provisioned working deployment | Promote/fence writers and redirect traffic |

Pilot light can't serve requests until you switch servers on and scale up; warm standby can take traffic immediately at reduced capacity and only needs to scale up. Hot standby is provisioned for full production load, so it doesn't depend on autoscaling working during a disaster, which AWS calls *static stability*.

Pros: simpler write ownership, if failover fences the old primary so only one writer remains authoritative. Cons: the standby is paid for but idle, users far from the primary get high latency, and **failover is a rarely exercised, risky operation**. Many outages get worse because failover itself fails: stale runbooks, DNS TTLs that don't expire as expected, untested capacity in the standby.

> [!warning] Untested failover isn't failover
> Exercise failover and restore procedures on a schedule appropriate to the system, including controlled production traffic shifts where justified. Verify fencing, recovery point, routing, capacity and rollback.

> [!note] Replication isn't backup
> Cross-region replication faithfully copies mistakes too. Logical deletions and corrupting writes can propagate to replicas. Keep tested backups and retained logs, with appropriately isolated access. The latest recoverable good state depends on available backups, logs and the incident; an RPO is a target, not simply the age of one backup.

### Recovering before a damaging change

If a faulty migration's deletes already reached the standby, promoting it does not recover the rows. Point-in-time recovery needs a suitable base backup and retained recovery logs to reconstruct the state just before the change. Later legitimate writes then need extraction and reconciliation; restoring old state discards them. Independently restricted backup access can reduce the chance that the same mistake or credential destroys both production state and its recovery material. Test restore integrity and duration, not just whether backup files exist.

## Key takeaways
- Standby warmth changes how much provisioning and capacity work remains during recovery.
- Fence the old writer, validate the standby and exercise routing, capacity and rollback.
- Replication copies bad writes as well as good ones; restore from a good base state plus retained logs when needed.
- Assess recoverable good state and reconciliation against the RPO rather than equating it to backup age.

## Further reading
- [AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html)
- [PostgreSQL: Continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/continuous-archiving.html)

questions.prompt: At 14:02 a faulty migration deletes 30% of rows in your primary database in eu-west-1. It replicates asynchronously to a warm standby in eu-central-1 with about 1 s of lag. Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Assume the deletion has already reached the standby before failover is considered.

options.text: Failing over to eu-central-1 recovers the deleted rows.
options.explanation: Wrong. The deletes replicated within about a second, so the standby is missing the same rows.

options.text: You need a point-in-time restore using a suitable base backup plus retained recovery logs to a moment just before 14:02.
options.explanation: Correct. Point-in-time recovery from backups plus the write-ahead log can restore to just before the bad migration.

options.text: The recoverable state depends on retained good backups and logs, corruption timing and reconciliation; the RPO is the target against which recovery is assessed.
options.explanation: Neither observed replication lag nor backup cadence alone guarantees a recovery point for logical corruption.

options.text: Writes made after 14:02 must be reconciled after the restore, because a point-in-time restore discards them.
options.explanation: Correct. Rows written after the restore point have to be replayed or merged deliberately.

options.text: Separate-account backups with independently restricted access can reduce the chance that one mistake or credential deletes both production data and backups.
options.explanation: Isolation helps only if permissions and recovery controls enforce it; a separate account label alone does not prevent cross-account deletion.

questions.workedExample:
1. Replication copies *everything*, including deletes. The standby is equally broken.
2. Recovery: restore a snapshot, replay the WAL to 14:01:59.
3. Data written between 14:02 and the restore must be extracted and reconciled.
4. Assess the actual recoverable good state and reconciliation loss against the recovery objective.
5. Separate accounts guard against 'delete the backups too'.

lessons.title: Reserving active-region capacity and ownership
lessons.summary: Explain survivor headroom and route invariant-sensitive writes to a fenced authoritative owner.
lessons.body:
Active-passive prepares standby capacity. Active-active serves live traffic in every region, but each survivor must still absorb failures without inventing extra capacity.

## Active-active

Every region serves live traffic. Users are routed to the nearest healthy region (latency-based DNS, anycast, or a global load balancer).

```
  EU users         US users
     |                |
 [Region EU] <----> [Region US]
  reads +    async    reads +
  writes   replicate  writes
```

Pros: local serving can reduce latency and each region exercises a production path. Failure routing, data promotion and spare-capacity behavior still need separate tests; active-active does not exercise every failover scenario.

Cons: if both regions accept writes to the **same data**, you must handle **conflicts**. And each region needs spare capacity to absorb the other's traffic. In the simplest model (equal regions, equally loaded, load divides linearly), when one of N regions fails its traffic is shared by the N − 1 survivors, the surviving capacity sets an ideal ceiling on normal utilisation:

```formula reference
U_max = (N − 1) / N
where
U_max: the ideal normal utilisation ceiling of each region, as a fraction of its capacity
N: the number of equal active regions, at least 2
%: per cent; 0.5 = 50 %
In words: reserve enough capacity for all surviving regions to absorb one failed region’s load. More equal regions share that extra load more widely; real deployments need further operating margin.
```

With two regions, each must stay at or below 50% before losing one. Real designs need margin below this and must account for state, retries, caches and resource-specific bottlenecks.

### Avoiding conflicts: partition the writes

The simplest active-active design gives each piece of data a **home region**:

- A user's account lives in the region where they signed up; all writes for that user go there.
- Other regions can serve **reads** from asynchronous replicas, and forward writes to the home region.
- One authoritative writer avoids concurrent cross-region ownership if enforced through failover fencing. Local transactions still need concurrency control, and multi-record operations can require coordination.

This is often called *geo-partitioning*. CockroachDB, Spanner and DynamoDB-based designs commonly use it, and it lines up neatly with data residency.

### Browsing and reservation can differ

Ticket-seat browsing may use global replicas when the product accepts delayed availability. Selling a seat needs an atomic condition that admits exactly one successful reservation. Route that operation to its fenced home-region writer, or use a suitable consensus-based store with conditional updates. Strong reads alone do not serialise a later write. Preallocated exclusive seat ownership is another possibility, but transferring ownership must preserve the exclusivity rule.

## Key takeaways
- Active serving in every region does not exercise every failure-routing scenario.
- Equal regions need spare capacity for the failed region's load; the ideal ceiling still needs operating margin.
- A home region gives each record one write owner while other regions can serve delayed read copies.
- Hard reservation invariants still require atomic conditions or transactions, not a fresh read followed by an unconditional write.

## Further reading
- [Azure Architecture Center: Geode pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/geodes)
- [AWS: DynamoDB global tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html)

questions.prompt: Two active regions have equal capacity. Load tests show that either one alone cannot sustain the combined admitted traffic. One fails and all traffic moves to the survivor, with no immediate extra capacity or load shedding. What follows?

options.text: The survivor overloads; active serving in both regions still requires reserved capacity for a failure.
options.explanation: Correct. The supplied load test establishes that the survivor lacks capacity for all transferred traffic.

options.text: The surviving region’s load remains unchanged because a load balancer spreads traffic evenly.
options.explanation: Wrong. The survivor now gets both regions' traffic. The load balancer can't spread it to a region that's down.

options.text: The failed region’s traffic is automatically discarded, so the survivor stays at its old load.
options.explanation: Wrong. That defeats the purpose of active-active. Routing will send failed-region users to the survivor.

options.text: Active-active doesn't need spare capacity because both regions are already serving traffic.
options.explanation: Wrong. Serving traffic in both regions removes the idle *standby*, but each region still needs headroom for the other's load during failure.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both regions’ traffic moves onto one region’s capacity in the stated failure.
2. The survivor cannot sustain the supplied combined demand, so queueing or rejection increases.
3. Reserve standing headroom for failover and account for retries, cache misses and other shared limits.
4. Use controlled traffic shifts and admission limits so overload does not cascade.

questions.prompt: A global ticketing platform must never sell the same seat twice, and wants low-latency browsing worldwide. Which data architecture fits best?

options.text: Active-active with multi-region writes and last-writer-wins for seat records.
options.explanation: Wrong. LWW would silently discard one of two concurrent sales. Both buyers get a confirmation and the seat is double-sold.

options.text: Replicate seat maps for browsing; reserve through a fenced authoritative owner or suitable consistent store using an atomic condition or transaction.
options.explanation: Correct when delayed browsing is acceptable. The atomic reservation enforces uniqueness; fresh reads or a single endpoint alone do not make a later unconditional write safe.

options.text: Use CRDT sets so each region can add seat sales independently and merge later.
options.explanation: Wrong. CRDTs guarantee convergence, not invariants. Both sales would merge into the set, still selling the seat twice.

options.text: Active-passive, with all browsing and purchases served from one region.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's correct for the invariant, but browsing from one region gives distant users high latency, which fails the second requirement.

questions.workedExample:
1. Browsing can use replicated views if the product accepts delayed availability.
2. Reservations need an atomic condition or transaction enforcing one successful reservation per seat; a fresh read followed by an unconditional write is insufficient.
3. Route to a fenced authoritative owner, or use an appropriate strongly consistent store with conditional updates.
4. Measure latency and decide the product budget; no fixed global reservation RTT is asserted.
5. Preallocated exclusive seat ownership is another possible design, with coordinated transfer.

questions.prompt: Four equal active regions share traffic evenly. The design must survive one region failing without adding capacity immediately. Which planning rule is sound?

options.text: The current average CPU alone proves failover is safe.
options.explanation: Average CPU omits routing skew, resource-specific bottlenecks and changed demand during recovery.

options.text: Every region can run at full capacity because the others will absorb its traffic.
options.explanation: The survivors then have no capacity left for transferred work.

options.text: Active-active removes the need to exercise failure routing.
options.explanation: Normal serving does not test every failure path or ownership transition.

options.text: Reserve enough standing capacity for the survivors to carry all admitted work, then leave margin for skew, retries and cold caches.
options.explanation: Correct. Sharing across more survivors reduces each one’s extra share in the ideal model, but the actual bottlenecks still need testing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Remove a region from the capacity plan.
2. Route its work to the surviving regions using the intended failure policy.
3. Check that every relevant resource can handle the resulting demand, including recovery effects.
4. Validate with load and failover tests; region count alone does not prove safety.

lessons.title: Choosing multi-writer conflict semantics
lessons.summary: Compare LWW, CRDT merge and application resolution while keeping hard invariants explicit.
lessons.body:
Home-region ownership avoids concurrent regional writes to one record. When local writes to that same record are required in several regions, choose the conflict semantics deliberately.

## Conflict handling across regions

### When you must accept multi-region writes: conflict handling

If two regions can write the same record concurrently (DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra multi-DC, CouchDB, multi-primary MySQL), concurrent writes will collide. Options:

1. **Last-writer-wins (LWW)**: keep the write with the highest timestamp. Simple, and what DynamoDB global tables do in their default, eventually consistent mode, but it **silently discards** the other write, and clock skew can make the "wrong" one win. (Since 2025 DynamoDB also offers a multi-Region *strongly* consistent mode for global tables, which rejects overlapping cross-Region writes with a retryable conflict error and adds cross-region communication latency.)
2. **Merge by data type**: use **CRDTs** (conflict-free replicated data types) that converge under their required delivery and merge assumptions, including eventual exchange of updates: counters (each region increments its own slot; reading combines the slots), sets with add/remove semantics, registers with defined rules. Riak and Redis Enterprise's active-active mode use CRDTs.
3. **Application-level resolution**: keep both versions (siblings) and let the application or the user merge them, as with conflicting edits in a document.
4. **Avoid it for invariants**: anything with a hard constraint (account balance must not go negative; one seat sold once) usually uses a single writer or a consensus-based store (Spanner, CockroachDB). Some bounded invariants can instead use escrow: preallocate disjoint spending or stock rights to regions, and reject locally when rights run out. Transferring rights then requires coordination.

The counter CRDT (often called a G-Counter, a grow-only counter) is the simplest to see. Each region only ever increases its own slot, and merging two copies takes the larger value of each slot, so repeated state merges do not double-count increments, provided stable identifiers for replicas and durable-state rules hold:

Each replica increases only its own durable slot. Merge two copies by keeping the larger value for each slot, then add the slots to read the total. Repeated delivery of the same counter state does not add the increment again.

If one copy has {EU: 41, US: 60} and another has {EU: 40, US: 62}, the merge is {EU: 41, US: 62}, and the counter reads 103.

> [!example] Shopping basket vs bank balance
> A basket can use a CRDT with chosen add/remove semantics, but quantities, checkout, deletion and inventory constraints still need explicit product rules. Convergence alone does not bound every bad outcome. An ordinary mergeable balance counter cannot safely let both regions independently approve £100 against the same £150 balance. Escrow can partition spending rights, but neither region may spend beyond its allocation. Route balance updates to the account's fenced home region, or use a strongly consistent store, and atomically validate and apply each debit.

### Counter identity and decrements

A grow-only counter needs stable unique replica identities, durable slots and atomic local increments. Delivery retries are deduplicated separately from the state merge. To represent decrements, a PN-Counter combines two grow-only counters and reads their difference: total increments minus total decrements. That still does not enforce one like per user without separate identity rules. During a partition totals can disagree without a fixed small bound, then converge after updates are eventually exchanged.

DynamoDB's MREC mode resolves conflicts per item, including different-attribute updates; it does not provide an attribute-wise merge. MRSC is a separately configured strongly consistent mode. Current AWS documentation permits combinations of three supported Regions, including Regions on different continents. You cannot change a global table's consistency mode after creation, so adopting MRSC for an existing EU/US MREC table still requires a migration rather than an in-place switch.

## Key takeaways
- LWW resolves a conflict by discarding one competing write; it does not merge independent whole-item edits.
- CRDT convergence relies on the data type's identity, durable state, merge and eventual-delivery assumptions.
- A counter merge does not enforce one-like-per-user, non-negative balances or unique reservations.
- Use atomic authoritative operations or bounded exclusive rights for invariants that merge semantics cannot preserve.

## Further reading
- [AWS: DynamoDB global tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html)
- [Wikipedia: Conflict-free replicated data type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict-free_replicated_data_type)

questions.prompt: Your user profiles are stored in DynamoDB global tables replicated across eu-west-1 and us-east-1. A user updates their display name in the EU at the same moment a support agent in the US updates the same user's email address. Both write the whole item. What does DynamoDB global tables do by default?

options.text: It merges both changes field by field, so the item ends up with the new name and the new email.
options.explanation: Wrong. Global tables don't merge fields. Conflicting writes to the same item are resolved for the item as a whole.

options.text: It applies last-writer-wins: one whole-item write survives and the other's change is silently lost.
options.explanation: Correct. Global tables (in their default multi-region eventual consistency mode) reconcile concurrent writes with last-writer-wins, so one of the two updates disappears with no error.

options.text: It rejects the second write with a conflict error.
options.explanation: Wrong. Both regions accept the writes locally. The conflict is resolved later during replication, without errors to either writer.

options.text: It keeps both versions as siblings for the application to resolve.
options.explanation: Wrong. That's the Riak/Dynamo-paper approach, not DynamoDB global tables.

questions.workedExample:
1. EU writes `{name: 'Sam', email: old}`; US writes `{name: old, email: new}` at the same moment.
2. Each region accepts its own write locally and replicates asynchronously.
3. Conflict resolution: the write with the later timestamp wins everywhere.
4. Outcome: either the new name or the new email is lost.
5. Mitigations:
   - UpdateItem does not give attribute-wise merging across MREC Regions: conflicts are resolved per item, so different attributes can still lose updates.
   - Route writes for a user to their home region.
   - Choose an appropriate strongly consistent design if needed. Current AWS documentation permits MRSC tables using three supported Regions, including cross-continent combinations. A global table's consistency mode cannot be changed after creation, so this existing MREC table still needs a migration rather than an in-place switch.

questions.prompt: You need a global "likes" counter per post that every region can increment locally, with no lost increments, even during a network partition. Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Assume each replica has a stable unique identity, durable counter state and atomic local increments; application retries are deduplicated separately.

options.text: A G-Counter CRDT works: each region increments only its own slot, and the value is the sum of all slots.
options.explanation: Correct. Merging takes the maximum of each slot, which is commutative and idempotent, so all replicas converge without losing increments.

options.text: Last-writer-wins on a single integer works just as well.
options.explanation: Wrong. If EU writes 101 and US writes 101 from 100, LWW keeps one 101, losing an increment.

options.text: A PN-Counter can represent increments and decrements using two G-Counters, whose value is total increments minus total decrements; one-like-per-user needs separate identity semantics.
options.explanation: This is one counter design, not the only way to implement likes/unlikes. Retried user actions and duplicate likes need additional modeling.

options.text: Totals may differ without a fixed small bound during a partition, then converge once updates are eventually exchanged.
options.explanation: Correct. That's the eventual consistency you accept for availability and local writes.

options.text: An ordinary unconstrained G-Counter alone enforces a global limit of 1,000 accepted increments.
options.explanation: Ordinary convergence does not enforce a cap. Escrow/bounded-counter designs can preallocate rights for local operations, with safe coordination to transfer rights.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each replica increments its own stable, durable slot.
2. Merge replicas by keeping the highest value for each slot, then combine the slots.
3. Repeated state merges do not add the same increment twice; application request retries still need deduplication.
4. Separate grow-only counters can track increments and decrements.
5. Neither ordinary convergence nor a grow-only counter enforces a global cap or one action per user.

lessons.title: Placing data inside isolated cells
lessons.summary: Apply an explicit residency requirement to every copy and contain local operational failures with cells.
lessons.body:
Regional replication and conflict rules do not contain every bad deploy or runaway tenant. Combine home-region placement with smaller independent stacks and audit every data-copy path.

## Data residency

Consider a hypothetical tenant whose contract explicitly requires EU-only storage and processing. The following is an architecture exercise for that stated requirement.

- **Pin data to a region by tenant or user**: EU customers' records live and are processed in EU regions, and are not replicated to the US.
- **Separate global from local data**: product catalogues and configuration can be global; personal data stays local. A global directory can map opaque tenant identifiers to home regions, but identifiers and routing metadata may themselves be personal data if they can be linked to a person; minimise and govern that data too.
- **Watch the side channels**: backups, logs, analytics pipelines, search indexes, caches and support tools all copy data. Residency applies to every copy.
- **Disaster recovery inside the boundary**: fail over from Frankfurt to another EU region, not to Virginia.

## Cell-based architecture

Multi-region protects you from a *region* failing. But many outages are caused by **you**: a bad deploy, a poison-pill request, a runaway tenant, a configuration change. Shared dependencies can let such failures affect many customers.

A **cell-based architecture** divides the system into many independent, identical copies called **cells**, each serving a subset of customers, with no shared state between cells.

```
         [ thin cell router ]
        /    |    |    |     \
   [cell1][cell2][cell3]...[cellN]
   each: own app tier, DB, cache, queues
   customers mapped to one cell
```

- **Blast radius**: a cell-local failure can be contained to that cell if shared dependencies remain healthy. With 20 equally populated cells, one cell holds 5% of customers.
- **Staged deploys**: roll out to one cell, watch, then expand in waves.
- **Known scaling limits**: each cell has a fixed maximum size that has been load tested. Growth means adding cells, not scaling one system into unknown territory.
- **Routing layer**: a thin, extremely simple router (often a lookup of customer → cell) is a shared dependency to keep minimal and robust; audit other shared services and control-plane dependencies too.

AWS uses cells extensively (it publishes guidance on the pattern), Slack migrated to a cellular architecture aligned with availability zones after zone-level incidents, and Azure calls the pattern **Deployment Stamps**. A related AWS technique, **shuffle sharding**, assigns each customer to a random combination of a few nodes, so that one customer's poison traffic overlaps fully with very few others.

Cells and regions combine: each region contains several cells; a customer's cell lives in their home region; DR replicates each cell to a paired region.

## Putting it together

A realistic design for a global SaaS:

1. Users are assigned a **home region** (by residency or proximity) and a **cell** within it.
2. A global directory and router send requests to the right cell, wherever the user connects.
3. Each cell replicates asynchronously to a standby in a paired region inside the same jurisdiction (define objectives and verify recovery point and duration with drills).
4. Truly global data (catalogue, feature flags) is replicated everywhere, read-mostly.
5. Invariant-critical operations stay single-writer; commutative data (likes, presence, baskets) can be multi-writer with CRDTs.

### Why shuffled assignments reduce full overlap

With fixed groups of four workers, a customer's traffic that breaks all four removes every worker for its whole group. Shuffle sharding instead assigns customers different four-worker combinations drawn from the larger fleet. Another customer loses every assigned worker only when its combination fully overlaps the failed one; partial overlaps can leave a healthy retry route. This comparison assumes independent uniform assignments. It does not guarantee that every partially overlapping customer has spare capacity or that shared dependencies survive.

## Key takeaways
- A stated residency boundary covers backups, logs, analytics, search, caches and support paths as well as the primary.
- Cells isolate full serving stacks and bound tested scale; shared routers and control planes still require scrutiny.
- Staged cell deployment and tenant isolation reduce impact only when failures stay within the intended boundary.
- Shuffle sharding reduces full overlap between assigned worker sets, assuming healthy retry alternatives and sufficient capacity.

## Further reading
- [AWS: What is a cell-based architecture?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture/what-is-a-cell-based-architecture.html)
- [AWS Builders' Library: Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/workload-isolation-using-shuffle-sharding/)
- [Slack: Slack's migration to a cellular architecture](https://slack.engineering/slacks-migration-to-a-cellular-architecture/)
- [Azure Architecture Center: Deployment Stamps pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/deployment-stamp)

questions.prompt: An EU healthcare customer requires that patient data never leaves the EU. Your platform runs in eu-central-1 and us-east-1. Which copies of data must you check? Select all that apply.

options.text: Database backups and snapshots, including cross-region DR copies.
options.explanation: Correct. Backups are full copies of personal data. Automatic cross-region snapshot copy to us-east-1 would breach the requirement.

options.text: Application logs and error-tracking events that include request payloads.
options.explanation: Correct. Logs often contain names, IDs or health details and are frequently shipped to a central (possibly US) logging service.

options.text: The search index and caches built from patient records.
options.explanation: Correct. Derived copies are still personal data. A global search cluster or a cache in the US would break residency.

options.text: The global product catalogue of software features, which contains no personal data.
options.explanation: Wrong. Data without personal information isn't in scope for this requirement, so it can be replicated globally.

options.text: Analytics events flowing into the data warehouse.
options.explanation: Correct. Analytics pipelines frequently centralise data. Events about EU patients must be processed and stored in EU-resident infrastructure.

questions.workedExample:
1. Residency applies to *every* copy of in-scope data, not just the primary database.
2. List the places data flows: primary DB, replicas, backups, DR copies, caches, search indexes, queues, logs, traces, analytics, support tools, third-party processors.
3. For each, ask: does it contain patient data, and where is it stored or processed?
4. Keep EU tenants' cells, backups and DR pairs inside the EU (e.g. Frankfurt ↔ Ireland), and scrub or regionalise logs and analytics.
5. The catalogue has no personal data, so it's out of scope.
6. Answer: 0, 1, 2 and 4.

questions.prompt: A SaaS company already runs in three regions, yet most of its major outages last year were caused by bad deploys and one large customer's runaway workload, each affecting every customer in a region. Which change most directly reduces the impact of these incidents?

options.text: Add a fourth region.
options.explanation: Wrong. The incidents weren't regional infrastructure failures. A bad deploy or noisy tenant would hit the fourth region's customers in the same way.

options.text: Move to a cell-based architecture: split each region into independent, size-capped cells with no shared state, map each customer to one cell, and deploy to cells in waves.
options.explanation: Cell isolation and staged deployment reduce potential impact, provided dependencies are isolated and monitoring catches the problem before rollout expands.

options.text: Switch from active-passive to active-active.
options.explanation: Wrong. Active-active changes how regions share traffic. Within each region, every customer still shares the same deployment and the same noisy neighbours.

options.text: Increase the size of each region's database.
options.explanation: Wrong. More capacity may delay saturation from the runaway tenant, but it doesn't isolate it and does nothing about bad deploys.

questions.workedExample:
1. Classify the incidents: self-inflicted (deploys) and noisy neighbour (one tenant). Neither is a region outage.
2. Multi-region protects against region failure; what's needed is isolation *within* regions.
3. Cells: say 10 cells per region, each a full stack (app, DB, cache, queues), sized to a tested maximum.
   - Bad deploy → one first-wave cell among 30 equally populated cells contains about 1/30 of customers; detection and safe rollback are still required.
   - Runaway tenant → only its cell's customers are affected; move it to a dedicated cell.
4. Keep the cell router very thin and static (customer → cell lookup) to reduce, not eliminate, shared failure risk.
5. Shuffle sharding can shrink overlap between customers even further.

questions.prompt: A service has 100 workers. With plain sharding, customers are split into 25 groups of 4 workers each, and one customer's poison requests crash all 4 workers in its group. With shuffle sharding, each customer is instead assigned a random combination of 4 of the 100 workers. Why is the blast radius so much smaller? Assume independent uniform assignments and enough surviving worker capacity for retries.

options.text: Shuffle sharding gives each customer more workers, so the bad customer can't crash them all.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each customer still has 4 workers, and the poison customer still crashes its own 4.

options.text: Other customers rarely share the entire failed worker set, so partial overlap can leave healthy assigned workers for retries.
options.explanation: Correct. In plain sharding, everyone in the bad group loses all their workers. In shuffle sharding, most customers overlap with the bad customer on at most one or two workers, so retries reach healthy ones.

options.text: Shuffle sharding detects and blocks poison requests automatically.
options.explanation: Wrong. It doesn't recognise bad requests; it limits how many others share the same fate.

options.text: It moves the bad customer to a different region.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's an assignment scheme within a fleet, not cross-region routing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Fixed worker groups make all customers in a group share the same complete failure set.
2. Shuffled assignments give different customers different combinations.
3. Partial overlap can leave a healthy assigned worker for retries; full overlap is much rarer.
4. The benefit depends on healthy retry alternatives, available capacity and isolated shared dependencies.
